mcqs.question: Why can the internet support far more simultaneous users on the same physical links than a circuit-switched network of equal capacity could?
options: Packets are compressed more efficiently than circuit-switched voice data
Packet switching uses a faster physical signaling standard than circuit switching
Statistical multiplexing lets many flows share a link opportunistically, using capacity that a reserved, dedicated circuit would leave idle between bursts
Routers cache packets so the same data never has to be sent twice
mcqs.explanation: The efficiency gain is purely about how capacity is shared: statistical multiplexing lets idle moments from one flow be used by another, whereas a circuit's reserved capacity sits unused during silence. Compression, signaling speed, and caching aren't what distinguishes the two switching paradigms.

mcqs.question: A financial exchange needs a guaranteed, fixed sub-millisecond latency link between two data centers with no variance. Which switching model fits, and why?
options: Packet switching, because statistical multiplexing always produces lower average latency
Packet switching, because packets can be rerouted to whichever path is currently fastest
Neither model can guarantee fixed latency under any circumstances
Circuit switching, because it reserves dedicated capacity so the path's latency doesn't vary with other traffic's load
mcqs.explanation: Circuit switching's dedicated, unshared path is exactly what removes latency variance from contention — the trade this scenario needs. Packet switching's shared links mean latency varies with queuing under load, and dynamic rerouting to the fastest path doesn't produce a fixed guarantee, it produces adaptability instead.

mcqs.question: Which of the four delay components is the one that varies unpredictably based on real-time network load, rather than being roughly fixed for a given path and packet size?
mcqs.explanation: Queuing delay depends on how many other packets are already waiting at a router's buffer at that instant — pure real-time congestion, and hence unpredictable. Propagation and transmission delay are set by physical distance and link rate/packet size; processing delay is typically near-constant router overhead.

mcqs.question: A user upgrades from 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps home internet but says their competitive online game still feels just as laggy. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The upgrade didn't actually take effect, since more bandwidth always reduces perceived lag
Bandwidth (capacity) and latency (delay) are different measurements; the game's lag is dominated by round-trip latency to the game server, which a bandwidth upgrade doesn't change
Gigabit connections have inherently higher latency than slower connections
The router needs to be replaced to take advantage of the new bandwidth for gaming specifically
mcqs.explanation: Gaming is a small-packet, frequent-round-trip workload, so it's latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound — more bandwidth doesn't shrink the physical propagation delay to the game server. There's no general rule that gigabit links have higher latency (the higher-latency-for-gigabit claim), and the scenario gives no reason to suspect the upgrade failed or that hardware is the bottleneck.
